t: LeetCode 1516 — Move Sub-Tree of N-Ary Tree
o: Node p must become the LAST child of q, and we return the possibly-new root. Three relationships exist: q inside p’s subtree (case 1 — moving p naively disconnects the tree, so q must first be cut from its own parent; if p was the root, q becomes the new root), p inside q’s subtree or fully disjoint (cases 2 and 3 — simply detach p and append it to q). Example 4 illustrates case 1 with p = root, producing root q; example 3 shows the disjoint move; example 2 shows the no-op where p is already q’s child. All mutations are cheap pointer/list edits once the parents of p and q are known.
k: Only one membership test is needed: whether q lies in p’s subtree — if p lies in q’s subtree the required surgery is identical to the disjoint case.
In case 1 detach q from its parent before attaching p beneath q; if p was the root, q is returned as the new root.
The problem states p already being a direct child of q means no change, so guard that case explicitly.

a.n: Approach 1: Parent Map Plus Membership DFS
a.i: One traversal records every node’s parent; a second traversal started at p tests whether q is reachable, i.e., whether q lives in p’s subtree. Armed with parentP, parentQ and that boolean, the rewiring is uniform: detach p, optionally detach q, append p to q.
s: Iteratively traverse from root storing parent[child] for every edge.
If parent[p] is q, return root unchanged.
Run a DFS from p to determine qInP.
Remove p from parentP.children when parentP exists; if qInP, also remove q from parentQ.children.
Append p to q.children; return q if p was the root, otherwise root.
a.t: O(n) — two linear traversals plus O(degree) list removals.
a.sp: O(n) — parent map plus the explicit stacks.

a.n: Approach 2: Single-Pass DFS with Enter/Exit Events
a.i: During one depth-first walk, q lies in p’s subtree exactly when q is visited between entering p and leaving p. Pushing an exit marker for each node onto an explicit stack creates that window: a flag insideP turns on when p is entered and off when its exit marker pops, and seeing q while insideP is set proves containment. Parents are captured along the way, so everything completes in a single traversal.
s: Process (node, closing) events from a stack; push the exit marker before pushing children.
On enter: set insideP when node is p; record qInP if node is q while insideP.
While scanning children, capture parentP and parentQ.
Apply the same guard and detach/attach rules; return q only when p was the root.
a.t: O(n) — one traversal; removals are bounded by list degrees.
a.sp: O(n) — the event stack holds at most all nodes plus exit markers.

w: Spell out the three cases before touching code — the case analysis is what earns points here. Pitfalls: modifying children lists mid-traversal (finish discovery first), forgetting that p may be the root so q becomes the answer, skipping the already-a-child guard, and appending p to q before removing q from its old parent in case 1. Edge cases: q a direct child of p, p adjacent to the root, deeply skewed chains (iterative stacks avoid recursion limits). Likely follow-ups: support batched moves, or achieve O(depth) membership checks given upward parent pointers.
